Another viral story based on bad intelligence. If you want journalism that's
written for you rather than clicks or awards, please become a paid subscriber
(or chip in to my [GoFundMe here](https://www.gofundme.com/f/bcatm9-testing).)

U.S. intelligence never concluded that Alice Huang was a spy, sources tell me.

How, then, did the media get so spun up over a made-for-Hollywood story about
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang getting honeypotted by a Chinese spy?

Blame Marco Rubio. He cooked the intelligence until it was charred beyond
recognition, then served it to the press -- just ahead of Pulitzer season.

Rubio, a China hawk and longtime foe of Huang's, took creative liberties in
describing preliminary intelligence and sent the media on a wild goose chase
that ended with Huang ousted from Nvidia.

Now the chatter in Washington is that the _New York Times_ will win a Pulitzer
for taking down the CEO of Nvidia and a powerful ally of President Trump's.
Never mind that its reporting was wrong, that Jensen Huang is back as CEO, or
that not a single national security official -- from the CIA and FBI Directors
to the Attorney General -- has said that Alice Huang was a spy.

The story was just too good.

## The Real Story

It began with eavesdropping. The U.S. intelligence community was conducting
routine foreign surveillance for technology theft by China, when it came
across Alice Huang. She was a Chinese national whose Singapore company,
Megaspeed, had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Jensen Huang was implicated when an NSA summary of intercepted communications
involving Alice Huang referred to an unnamed "U.S. Person." Though U.S. law
requires intelligence agencies to redact Americans' names for privacy reasons,
in some cases officials can ask to have them 'unmasked,' intel-speak for
'revealed.'

That unnamed American turned out to be Jensen Huang.

For a year and a half, Huang had been a thorn in the side of Washington's
China hawks. And he had something cabinet officials hate to see an outsider
have: a direct line to the President. Huang frequently dropped in at the White
House, dined with Trump at Mar-a-Lago, flew with him to Beijing on Air Force
One and was awarded the National Medal of Science by Trump.

## The Proxy War

Worst of all, in the hawks' eyes, Huang beat them in a battle pitting free
trade against national security. In December 2025, he talked Trump into
letting Nvidia sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China. In exchange, the U.S.
government would collect 25 percent of the chips' value. That deal drove
Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the defense hawks everywhere from
K Street to Silicon Valley up the wall.

"They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president," a former
administration official told the _Washington Post_.

Rubio's fight with Huang was a proxy for a broader fight with Commerce
Secretary Howard Lutnick, who had made himself Huang's chief protector inside
the administration. Lutnick, a Wall Street dealmaker with no patience for the
State Department's Cold War mindset, openly defended selling Nvidia chips to
China as a way to keep Chinese developers "addicted to the American technology
stack." Huang agreed.

Rubio sided with Bessent, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Defense
Secretary Pete Hegseth in favor of blacklisting companies suspected of
diverting Nvidia chips to China. Chief among them was Megaspeed, Alice Huang's
company. Lutnick resisted, warning it "will start a trade war with China."

Bessent finally vented in public, saying the rest of the government had wanted
Megaspeed blacklisted "for months." Then he pointed across town: "Commerce
holds the pen."

To Rubio's camp, Huang was the man whispering in the President's ear, and
Lutnick was the man doing what Huang wanted. Lutnick may have held the pen,
but Rubio had the ink, and he was willing to spill it by circulating
intelligence on the two Huangs' "close relationship" amid Nvidia's chip deals
with China.

## Raw Reporting

What the CIA and FBI actually had from the NSA intercepts and their own
collection was the messy, ambiguous stuff of routine counterintelligence.
Called "raw reporting," this is what intelligence analysts are trained to
handle with great caution because the information lacks context and
verification. Imagine what your text messages would sound like if someone read
portions without context.

Politicians, though, treat raw reporting like dynamite.

The FBI had been looking at Alice Huang for more than a year, curious how a
former Beijing TV journalist had turned up in Singapore with the backing to
buy billions of dollars' worth of computing power. The intercepts reportedly
show that she had contact of some form with China's Ministry of State
Security, which seems plausible, but far from proof that she was a spy.
Successful Chinese businesspeople in Southeast Asia are routinely leaned on by
Beijing's security services, and few feel free to turn down a meeting.

The CIA's own officials, the _Washington_ _Post_ later reported, were not yet
convinced that the intercepts proved she was knowingly passing anything to
Beijing. What's more, if counterintelligence officials really believed that
the head of America's most important tech company was being manipulated by a
Chinese honeypot, the standard operating procedure is for the FBI to privately
warn him with what it calls a "defensive briefing."

But Huang never got one.

Other countries came up empty, too. Singapore, hardly soft on illegal tech
brokers, ran its own investigation. Authorities there detained Alice Huang and
held her passport for months, then gave it back and let her go.

"We were thorough with Alice Huang; we took her in, we investigated her, but
we eventually released her because there was no basis for further
prosecution," Singapore's Prime Minister, Lawrence Wong, said.

## The Marco Memo

None of that nuance survived the Rubio leak. Before Trump's May trip to
Beijing, Rubio authored a highly classified memo calling Alice Huang a Chinese
spy, which he then circulated to the administration and, eventually, the
media.

Even the _Washington_ _Post_ acknowledged that Rubio's memo recast "the
agency's [CIA's] reporting in his own more assertive terms."

Or, without the bullshit: he cooked the books.

Asked about his role in the leak and his position on Huang, Rubio declined
several times to answer questions.

It didn't matter. The supposed gist of the memo leaked and the story landed on
the front page of the _New York Times_ on October 29. The rest of the press
then piled on.

The problem is that no one in government who has actually seen the
intelligence will back Rubio up.

Start with the Justice Department and the FBI, the agencies that actually hold
the criminal case file. Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked when the
Justice Department learned she might be a Chinese asset. He rejected the
premise: "Nobody said that. I certainly haven't said that."

Blanche added that no conclusions had been reached by the department, by him
or by FBI Director Kash Patel "around who she is or is not." Patel, who
usually can't resist chiming in on anything, has been silent.

Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, was asked twice by CNN's
Dana Bash whether Alice Huang is a spy. Both times he declined to say she was.

Even Trump has undercut Rubio's leak. "I haven't heard that she was a spy," he
told Fox News when asked.

Vice President JD Vance says that the intelligence he has seen wasn't enough
for him or Trump to conclude Alice Huang worked for Beijing.

Even on Capitol Hill, where calling someone a Chinese spy is usually an easy
applause line, members of Congress privy to the intelligence briefings have
been unwilling to use the s-word.

Tom Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee and doesn't usually
hold back on China, responded to Nvidia's reinstatement of Huang on Monday
with a statement that conspicuously avoided using the word "spy."

Democrats on the intelligence committees haven't backed Rubio's version
either. Representative Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence
Committee, walked out of a classified briefing for Congress's top leaders and
told reporters he still didn't know whether Alice Huang had knowingly gathered
secrets for Beijing or was merely a "useful idiot."

The final word came Monday, when Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO. The
board said it had heard from senior levels of the U.S. government and, based
on what they told it, was confident Huang's return "poses no national security
risk."

Since its October 29 scoop, the _New York Times_ has published a behind-the-
scenes piece on how its reporters "broke open" the investigation.

Something broke, anyway.

On November 6, the _Times_ flatly reported that Alice Huang "was a spy for
China's Ministry of State Security," recruited "to collect intelligence on
Jensen Huang."

Now, in their passive-aggressive way, the _Times_ and other outlets are
backing away from that claim. Instead of admitting they got the story wrong,
they're running philosophical treatises asking, 'What even is a spy anyway?'
-- one of the funnier goalpost relocation maneuvers I've seen.

What even is journalism?
